newsitem.title: ICELAND: FEATURE - Icelandic hill farmer has seen it all before.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Icelandic hill farmer has seen it all before.

text.p: Filippus Hannesson sits on his farm high on the ridge above the main road watching countless jeeps take scientists and journalists across the black sand plain below Vatnajokul, Europe's largest glacier.
The intruders are anxiously waiting for a huge ice dam in the glacier to give way, releasing a torrent of water and ice which they believe will flood the southeast coast of Iceland.

It all began a week ago when a volcano under the glacier began to erupt, causing parts of the ice cap to melt. The melted water has filled the Grimsvotn subglacial lake to the brim, and scientists say it is only a matter of time before the glacier bursts under the pressure.
But Hannesson is a wise and patient man. Coy about his exact age, he claims to be almost 100 years old.
"It's drawing closer, the glacier is obviously rising, but it's impossible to say when it will flood. It could be days, weeks or months," he told Reuters on Tuesday.

Hannesson's sheep farm Nupsstadur is the closest holding to the peak of the Vatnajokul, nestled in the shadow of Mount Eystrafjell, which lies west of the part of the glacier known as Skeidararjokull.
The farm house stands together with a tiny, ancient chapel, one of the few grass-roofed churches remaining in Iceland. Both are listed as important historical sites.
Hannesson lives with his 89 year-old brother Eyolfur in the village where their family have farmed since the 18th century.

The farmer has one thing that the scientists don't -- experience. He can remember the last major flood from the Grimsvotn lake in 1938, when flood waters reached right up to the perimeter of the farm.
His father, a postman, was crossing the glacier from Skaftafell when the torrent broke loose.
"He heard loud sucking sounds and cracking. He said it was like a giant woman in labour, groaning and moaning," Hannesson laughed.
On that occasion, the floods brought ice blocks as large as houses crashing down onto the plain, crushing telephone poles and severing communications between the east and the west of the island.
Hannesson and his nine brothers and sisters rushed to save their flock at the risk of being sucked into the quagmire.
"We had to keep moving all the time, or we would have got stuck fast. Luckily, none of the sheep were killed," he said.
With his sparkling blue eyes and clear complexion, Hannesson looks not a day over 70. The two brothers tend the farm themselves, getting around the place in a 1954 yellow and red painted army jeep.
Their only other concessions to the 20th century are a tractor and a television set.
But amid all the fuss of the past week, Hannesson remains calm. "I'm not afraid. The flood won't come here," he said.
Teams of engineers are on 24-hour alert to save those roads, bridges and power lines that can be saved when the floods break. Seismologists, journalists, rescue teams, are all waiting.
All is now quiet beneath the massive and desolate glacier, but the silence is laden with tension.
The floods will make up their own mind, and with water levels under the lake rising by 10 metres (33 feet) a day, the answer will not be long in coming.
